vignette:
Patient Narrative: Mr. L.

Mr. L. is a 61-year-old married man, a bus driver for the city transit authority for the past 32 years, who presents for evaluation at the urging of his wife. He is a quiet, stocky man with a steady, deliberate way of speaking, though his hands often tremble slightly when he is not gripping something solid.

The story he tells begins not in a warzone, but in a parking lot. Three years ago, while on a short break between routes, Mr. L. was approached by two men. He had stopped at a convenience store in a neighborhood he knew well. He remembers the sun was low, casting long shadows. He does not remember what they said to him. He remembers the pain—a bright, white-hot explosion in his ribs, then his kidneys, then his face. He remembers the concrete scraping the skin off his knuckles as he tried to shield himself. He remembers the sound of his own breathing, ragged and wet.

They did not want his wallet. They did not want his bus. They wanted him to suffer. For what felt like an eternity but was likely less than ten minutes, they used a tire iron and their boots to break parts of him. They spoke in low, calm voices, describing what they would do next. Mr. L. says he went somewhere else in his mind, a place behind his eyes where the pain was just a faraway noise. He remembers the paramedics finding him, remembers the fluorescent lights of the ER, but the details of the next three days are a blur of morphine and the sound of his wife crying.

The physical wounds healed. Three cracked ribs, a fractured orbital bone, a shattered kneecap. He was back at work in six months. But the man who returned to the driver’s seat is not the same man who left it.

Mr. L. now drives with his back pressed hard against the seat, his eyes constantly flicking to the rearview mirror, not for passengers, but for headlights that linger too long. He avoids the neighborhood where it happened. He takes a fifteen-mile detour every shift to bypass that parking lot, a route that costs him thirty minutes of unpaid time. When passengers board, he no longer greets them. He watches their hands. If a man boards wearing a dark hoodie, Mr. L.’s throat closes. His heart hammers against his repaired ribs. He feels the phantom pressure of a boot on his neck. He has pulled the bus over three times in the last month, told the passengers there was a mechanical issue, just so he could step outside, put his hands on his knees, and try to breathe.

At home, he is a ghost. He sleeps in the recliner in the basement, a baseball bat within arm’s reach. He has not slept in his marital bed in two years. His wife, a gentle woman who works as a librarian, says he flinches when she touches his shoulder. He has not been able to tolerate the sensation of a blanket or sheet touching his feet and ankles since the attack—it makes him feel trapped, like his legs are being pinned. He has stopped watching television; the sound of a car door slamming in a movie sends him into a cold sweat.

He describes a constant, low-grade feeling that something terrible is about to happen. He cannot explain it. He just knows it is coming. He feels cut off from his own life, as if he is watching a movie about a man who looks like him but feels nothing. He does not remember the last time he felt joy, or even contentment. His wife tells him their grandchildren ask why Grandpa looks so scared all the time. He has no answer for them.

Mr. L. sits in the office chair, his hands resting on his thighs, palms down. He stares at a spot on the wall. He says he came today because his wife made the appointment. He says he doesn’t think it will help, but he is tired of being afraid of the dark.
